questions.q: In "On Time," the speaker addresses Time as "envious" and "greedy." What does this personification reveal about the SPEAKER'S character, not Time's?
questions.a: The speaker reveals himself as morally discerning and spiritually confident — he sees through Time's apparent power to its essential emptiness ("mortal dross"). A wrong answer would describe Time's traits (e.g., "Time is jealous") instead of the speaker's judgment. This confusion shows the student cannot distinguish between the object described and the describing consciousness.

questions.q: The speaker in "On Shakespeare" asks: "What needs my Shakespear for his honour'd Bones / The labour of an age in piled Stones?" Explain in your own words what this rhetorical question reveals about the speaker's view of artistic legacy.
questions.a: The speaker believes true artistic greatness creates its own living monument in readers' minds ("live-long Monument") and needs no physical tomb. A wrong answer would focus on Shakespeare's bones or stones, missing that the speaker is articulating HIS OWN aesthetic philosophy: art's power lies in psychological impact, not material preservation. This error reveals the student conflates the subject (Shakespeare) with the speaker's interpretive stance.

questions.q: APPLY: In "On Time," the speaker says "Fly envious Time, till thou run out thy race." Rewrite this command as a declarative statement from the speaker's perspective that reveals his inner certainty. Example structure: "I know that..."
questions.a: "I know Time's power is temporary and self-destructive, while eternal joy is inevitable." Steps: 1) Identify the imperative "Fly" as the speaker's command. 2) Note "till thou run out thy race" implies Time's built-in limit. 3) Connect to the speaker's vision of "long Eternity" greeting "our bliss." 4) Synthesize: the command expresses certainty, not wishful thinking. A wrong answer would paraphrase the literal meaning ("Time should go away") without capturing the speaker's epistemological confidence.

questions.q: ANALYZE: Compare the speaker's relationship to the addressee in both poems. In "On Time," he commands Time; in "On Shakespeare," he questions Shakespeare. What does this contrast reveal about the speaker's intellectual hierarchy?
questions.a: The speaker positions himself as Time's judge (moral superior) but Shakespeare's awed student (intellectual inferior). He commands Time because he sees its limits; he questions Shakespeare because he recognizes Shakespeare's surpassing genius. A wrong answer would treat both addressees similarly (e.g., "he talks to both") missing the hierarchical distinction. This error shows inability to map tonal shifts onto the speaker's self-positioning.

questions.q: EVALUATE: A student claims: "The speaker in both poems is just Milton showing off his learning." Defend or refute using evidence from the poems' argumentative structure.
questions.a: Refute. In "On Time," the speaker constructs a logical progression: Time consumes false things → Time consumes itself → Eternity remains → Truth/Peace/Love shine. This is philosophical argument, not display. In "On Shakespeare," the speaker uses rhetorical questions to lead readers to a conclusion: Shakespeare's "easie numbers" (accessible verse) move hearts more than pyramids. The structure serves persuasion, not ego. A wrong answer would accept the claim or offer vague praise ("beautiful language") without analyzing argumentative architecture.

questions.q: CREATE: Write a 4-line stanza where the speaker from "On Time" addresses a modern distraction (social media, exams, FOMO) using the same personification and moral certainty. Maintain Milton's syntactic inversion (verb before subject) at least once.
questions.a: Example: "Scroll anxious Phone, till thy battery die, / Call on the leaden-thumbed hours that creep; / Thy glowing glass holds no eternity, / Truth lives not in what thy notifications reap." Criteria: 1) Personifies the distraction as flawed. 2) Uses inversion ("Scroll anxious Phone"). 3) Contrasts temporal limit with eternal value. 4) Reveals speaker's moral clarity. A poor answer would lack inversion, miss the contrast, or sound like complaint rather than judgment.
